content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 13: SSRF, Request Routing, and HTTP Infrastructure Attacks. It builds practical understanding of Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Allow only the intended URL schemes and destinations, validate resolved addresses at connection time, handle redirects safely, and restrict server egress to reduce internal-resource exposure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) can be understood through this sequence: Parse destination → Allowlist scheme + host → Check connection boundary → Limit network egress. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 93.1 Server-side URL fetching; 93.2 Trusting user-controlled destinations; 93.3 Access to internal and restricted services; 93.4 Cloud metadata and internal resource exposure; 93.5 URL validation and destination restrictions; 93.6 Network egress controls and safe HTTP clients. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Allow only the intended URL schemes and destinations, validate resolved addresses at connection time, handle redirects safely, and restrict server egress to reduce internal-resource exposure.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
content_blocks.expected_output: Only HTTPS URLs with an explicitly approved hostname and the expected port pass this initial policy check.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This is not sufficient alone: resolve and validate addresses at connection time, re-check each redirect, account for DNS rebinding, and apply network egress controls.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Allow only the intended URL schemes and destinations, validate resolved addresses at connection time, handle redirects safely, and restrict server egress to reduce internal-resource exposure. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.

Allow only the intended URL schemes and destinations, validate resolved addresses at connection time, handle redirects safely, and restrict server egress to reduce internal-resource exposure.
